sources.news_title: Blanche withdraws Trump fund plan in writing, ahead of AG confirmation vote
sources.text:
Holdout senators back Blanche for AG after he formally withdraws Trump fund plan
Two Republican senators who had threatened to block Todd Blanche's confirmation as the next US attorney general, now say they are ready to offer their support.
The senators did so after Blanche, currently serving as the acting attorney general, formally withdrew President Donald Trump's plan for a fund that could have been used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.
"We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund," Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, the two holdout senators, said in a joint statement.
The move clears the way for Blanche to be confirmed to his job on a permanent basis.
The proposed $1.8bn "anti-weaponisation" fund was announced earlier this year to settle a lawsuit by Trump against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) over the leak of his tax returns.
It would have allowed Trump allies to claim compensation for what they say were politically motivated prosecutions by previous administrations.
A second concern held by the two holdout senators was that the deal also shielded the president, his family and their businesses from IRS audits of their past tax returns. They wanted the scope of that to be narrowed.
The US Senate judiciary committee has a meeting scheduled for Tuesday, which could include a vote on Blanche's nomination.
"We look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon" Tillis said.
Trump's Republican Party previously lacked the votes for confirmation of his attorney general nominee because Tillis and Cornyn were not sufficiently satisfied by verbal assurances from Blanche that the planned fund was dead.
Tillis had expressed concern that administration will revive the fund and said the president was still harbouring a plan to set up a "payout pot for punks".
He said the political impasse was "unfortunate" because he did consider Blanche, who is Trump's former personal lawyer, to be qualified for the attorney general job.
In a post on X late on Sunday, Blanche said he had "met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions".
Attached to Blanche's post was a copy of the written order signed by Blanche. The text says: "This Order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund."
It was also accompanied by an unsigned memo in which he said the IRS immunity would be limited to the "named parties in the lawsuit". The plaintiffs in the lawsuit were Trump, his two sons Donald Jr and Eric, and the Trump Organization.
The fund plan and the tax audit provision prompted alarm among Democrats - and some Republicans - who argued it could result in payment to people who were prosecuted over the US Capitol riot on 6 January 2021, including those convicted of assaulting police officers.
Following the backlash, Blanche abandoned the plan. A federal judge also blocked the fund and expressed concerns that it breached ethical guidelines.
Prior to Blanche's two posts on Sunday, Trump himself gave conflicting statements on the future of both the fund and his nomination of Blanche to be America's top law enforcement official.
On Friday, he said the fund was "dead", but he subsequently threatened over the weekend to put the plan back on the table if members of his party did not move to approve Blanche.
Tillis and Cornyn are due to leave the US Senate when their terms expire in January.
In recent days, Trump had said he was considering withdrawing Blanche's nomination to be attorney general because the process was stalled and renominating him once the pair were out of office.
But there was also a concern, as analysts pointed out, that if Democrats won the majority in the senate during the November midterm elections, it would most certainly doom Blanche's chances of becoming the 88th US Attorney General.

sources.news_title: Blanche Rescinds Fund, Reaches Deal With Cornyn On Confirmation
sources.text:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal order late Sunday terminating President Trump's $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund," reaching an agreement with a key Republican holdout senator that could clear the way for Blanche's confirmation as attorney general at a Senate Judiciary Committee vote scheduled for Tuesday.
The order, dated Sunday and posted alongside a statement from Blanche's office, states: "The Attorney General's May 18, 2026 Order establishing the Anti-Weaponization Fund ('Fund') is rescinded and shall have no force or effect." The order goes on to say that despite several "frivolous lawsuits" filed challenging the fund, and at least one court declining to dismiss those claims as moot, "this Order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund." Blanche's order also narrowed the scope of tax-related protections included in the broader settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS, clarifying that those protections apply only retroactively rather than to future tax filings.
Natalie Yezbick, a spokeswoman for Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, confirmed to CBS News that "Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice" regarding the fund and the settlement's scope. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., the other Republican whose objections had stalled Blanche's nomination, had not issued public comment as of Sunday night. Cornyn and Tillis, both members of the Judiciary Committee, had said their support for Blanche hinged on the administration formally rescinding the fund in writing, particularly given Trump's continued public support for the idea even after Blanche testified at a June hearing that the fund was "dead." Cornyn had specifically pressed Blanche during his July 15 confirmation testimony on whether any written agreement existed to modify the settlement, and Blanche's office said Sunday that he "stands by all of his July 15, 2026 Senate Judiciary Committee testimony," attaching a transcript of that exchange alongside the new order.
The reversal comes just a day after Trump escalated the standoff rather than resolving it. In a Truth Social post Saturday, Trump said that if Cornyn and Tillis continued blocking Blanche's confirmation, he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general indefinitely and "push hard to get the Anti-Weaponization Bill" passed into law instead, writing it would be "back on the table" and that "a lot of people like it." Tillis responded at the time that the threat proved Trump intended to "resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against," and said Blanche "will not be confirmed because of this reversal." Even hours before Sunday night's rescission order, Trump continued defending the fund concept to reporters, saying people facing charges connected to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack who could have benefited from the fund had "their lives destroyed" and describing it as "a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered."
Trump has separately said Cornyn and Tillis were "both upset because I wouldn't endorse them" in their own political races — Cornyn lost his Republican primary this spring to Trump-backed candidate Ken Paxton, while Tillis, a frequent Trump critic, announced last year he would not seek reelection. The underlying fund was created as part of a settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS, and lawmakers from both parties had raised concerns that people convicted in connection with the Jan. 6 riot could have been eligible for payments under it. Separately, Trump's attorneys notified a court Friday that they would appeal a judge's ruling that characterized the IRS settlement as an improper act of self-dealing; the judge had referred one of Trump's attorneys for potential disciplinary action in that ruling and criticized Blanche's own involvement in negotiating the settlement, given his prior work as Trump's personal defense attorney.
That Blanche moved to formally rescind the fund within roughly 24 hours of Trump's public threat to revive it suggests the acting attorney general, or officials working on his behalf, calculated that securing Cornyn's vote was more urgent than preserving the president's preferred negotiating posture, even at the risk of appearing to contradict Trump's own Saturday statements. The gap between Trump's Sunday afternoon defense of the fund's underlying purpose and Blanche's Sunday night order eliminating it entirely illustrates how quickly the administration's public position shifted once a path to confirmation became available. Tillis's continued silence as of Sunday night, in contrast to Cornyn's swift confirmation of a deal, leaves open whether both Republican holdouts have actually reached agreement or whether Cornyn's office moved ahead of a fully settled arrangement.
Attention in the coming hours is likely to center on whether Tillis publicly confirms the same agreement Cornyn's office has described, and on whether Tuesday's scheduled Judiciary Committee vote proceeds as planned with full Republican support. Continued monitoring of Trump's public statements in the aftermath of the rescission, given his defense of the fund's purpose just hours before it was eliminated, and the progress of the separate court appeal over the underlying IRS settlement are expected to remain central threads as Blanche's confirmation process reaches its final stages.

sources.news_title: Blanche rescinds fund for Trump allies after senators threaten to block his attorney general bid
Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche rescinds 'anti-weaponization' fund
Trump defends massive settlement for ‘great American Patriots’ of Jan. 6, attacks GOP senators
sources.text:
Trump defends massive settlement for ‘great American Patriots’ of Jan. 6, attacks GOP senators
President Donald Trump on July 31, 2026 defended his “anti-weaponization” settlement fund as he sought confirmation of his nominee for attorney general, Todd Blanche. In this photo, Trump looks on during a Cabinet meeting at the White House on May 27, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump defended his highly criticized, nearly $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” settlement fund on social media and in a Cabinet meeting Friday, as two key Republican senators withheld support for the president’s nominee for attorney general over Trump’s refusal to formally end the pot of money.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that the fund, in exchange for him dropping his $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS, would not benefit him, but rather “the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed by the Crooked Joe Biden Administration” after they participated in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.
On the first day of his second term, Trump commuted the prison sentences of 14 of the attack’s ringleaders and members of the paramilitary groups the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys. The president granted a “full, complete and unconditional pardon” to all others charged with crimes after the attack.
“Perhaps there has never been a group of people treated so badly in our Nation’s history. They are suffering still, many ruined, and I felt that they should be given compensation for what has been done to them,” Trump continued in a 254-word post.
He also attacked Texas GOP Sen. John Cornyn and said acting Attorney General Todd Blanche should be “immediately approved” as attorney general.
Cornyn and North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis, both members of the Senate Committee on the Judiciary, have refused to advance Blanche’s nomination from committee to the full Senate until Blanche, also Trump’s former personal defense lawyer, formally ends the “anti-weaponization” fund in writing.
Blanche, of Florida, maintains his comments before a House Appropriations subcommittee in June prove the administration ended the fund.
‘Legal and political albatross’
In a late morning statement on X, Tillis said Trump “made it clear today that the so-called Anti Weaponization Fund is still alive, which is exactly why we are attempting to formally end it.”
“While I never disagreed that the Biden Administration pursued a number of vindictive prosecutions related to January 6, the criminals who assaulted police officers and defiled our nation’s Capitol are not ‘great American patriots’ who are ‘victims of government abuse.’ Anyone who attacked law enforcement should still be in prison, not getting a check from the federal government,” Tillis wrote.
He added he and Cornyn are working with Blanche, whom he described as “forthright, thoughtful and patient,” on ending the fund.
“It’s a shame his confirmation has hit a snag only because an incompetent personal advisor to the President refuses to amend the bogus settlement. I will continue working in good faith to put an end this legal and political albatross and prevent any potential misallocation of taxpayer dollars,” Tillis wrote.
Tillis’ office did not respond to a question about the identity of the adviser the senator mentioned in the statement.
When being questioned by reporters at the Cabinet meeting at Camp David just over an hour later, Trump said Blanche should be confirmed as attorney general “forthwith” and that the fund is “dead.”
“But you know, I wish it weren’t. To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused. … and I’d like to see them compensated for the pain.”
The White House press office on Friday issued a press release linking to statements and quotes in support of Blanche from dozens of law enforcement associations, former Justice Department officials and Republican lawmakers.
Trump, Cornyn and Tillis
On Thursday, Trump threatened to pull Blanche’s nomination and leave him in an acting capacity until both Cornyn and Tillis leave office at year’s end.
Cornyn’s career in the Senate is ending after he lost in a runoff election in May to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom Trump endorsed.
Tillis announced last year he would not seek reelection after Trump threatened to find primary opponents to challenge the North Carolina Republican after he refused to support Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.
Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, had scheduled a committee vote on Blanche’s nomination for Thursday morning, but postponed the vote late Wednesday when it was clear Cornyn and Tillis were not yet satisfied.
The Judiciary Committee is split between 12 Republicans and 10 Democrats. All Democrats are expected to oppose Blanche, and a majority vote is required to advance Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate for confirmation.
Judge slammed Trump settlement
Trump’s settlement with the IRS faced opposition on multiple fronts, including in court.
In a July 13 order, the Florida federal judge in Trump’s IRS case slammed the president’s settlement with his own administration as using the presidency to “manipulate” the courts.
Lawyers for Trump, his two sons and the Trump Organization made public in a federal court filing Friday their plans to appeal a lower court order that bars them “from referring to the purported ‘settlement agreement’ … as evidence of a ‘settlement’ reached in this matter.”
The Justice Department’s announcement of the “anti-weaponization” fund in May immediately drew scrutiny from both sides of the aisle for the possibility that Jan. 6 defendants who assaulted police officers could reap a reward.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. and Frank Bisignano, the Internal Revenue Service’s chief executive officer, a position created by Trump, signed the settlement that Trump negotiated with his own administration officials for himself, his sons and the private Trump Organization.
Like Blanche, Woodward also had ties to Trump’s criminal cases prior to the president’s second term. Woodward represented Trump’s co-defendant Walt Nauta in the government’s 2023 case regarding classified material found at Mar-a-Lago.
Opposition to the “anti-weaponization” fund among Republicans snarled quick passage of an immigration enforcement package to fund Trump’s mass deportation agenda for the remainder of his term.
The settlement deal also includes immunity for Trump, his sons Don Jr. and Eric, and the Trump Organization from tax audits and enforcement connected to any tax information leaked by a government contractor in 2019. The contractor was prosecuted and sentenced to jail time in 2024.
Cornyn pressed Blanche on the tax immunity portion of the deal during a July 15 confirmation hearing. Blanche defended the terms as “typical” of settlements with the IRS.
Cornyn wrote on social media Thursday the president is “mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis.”
Former Department of Justice officials told committee Democrats the IRS settlement language was “mind-boggling,” during a July 22 forum hosted by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J.
Amelia Twyman contributed to this report.

The good news: Todd Blanche should win confirmation in the US Senate this week and fully succeed Pam Bondi as Attorney General. The bad news, at least for the White House: The anti-weaponization fund got spiked as the cost of doing business with John Cornyn and Thom Tillis.

Breaking overnight: The White House believes it has a deal with GOP senators to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee after days of frenzied negotiations.
Blanche issued a formal document stating that the order creating the controversial $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund is “rescinded” with “no force or effect.” A second document affirms Blanche’s confirmation hearing testimony on the limits of President Donald Trump’s tax audit immunity deal.
Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) had blocked Blanche’s path through the Judiciary Committee until the Justice Department formally agreed to narrow the immunity deal and scrap the weaponization fund.
It wasn't just Cornyn and Tillis that threatened to sink Blanche over the fund and immunity deals. Cornyn and Tillis, both of whom hold grudges with Trump for different reasons, sit on the Judiciary Committee, which has to vote to send Blanche's nomination to the full Senate. If both of them vote against Blanche, John Thune would have to override the committee to call the nomination to the floor. And that's where the real problem would have emerged:
Several Republicans who don’t serve on the Judiciary panel have raised concerns about Blanche’s nomination. The Cornyn deal could ease their objections as well. Some GOP senators have been relying on the Texas Republican’s judgment throughout the Blanche talks.
The anger over the two deals went well beyond Cornyn and Tillis. The Senate Republican caucus made that much clear months ago, concerned over the optics of the audit immunity as well as a lack of oversight over the anti-weaponization fund. Some had raised concerns about the back-door appropriation of the money through a lawsuit settlement rather than creating it through the budget process with congressional approval. It has been a sticking point for weeks between Senate Republicans and the White House.
Rather than risk a split over Blanche, Donald Trump apparently chose to pick his battles more carefully. Trump has yet to post anything about this on Truth Social, but as the WSJ points out, it will require Trump to agree to the withdrawal:
The fund, which could have been used to pay Trump allies, and the audit protections were a product of a controversial settlement between Trump and his own administration. That pact ended a lawsuit filed by the president against the Internal Revenue Service for a contractor’s illegal leak of his tax returns.
It isn’t clear whether the Justice Department’s new commitments are legally binding. The text of the deal creating the fund said that it could be changed only with agreement of all of the parties who signed it, including the IRS, the Justice Department and Trump in his personal capacity.
Neither the White House nor Sen. Thom Tillis (R., N.C.), the other key GOP holdout, immediately responded to requests for comment.
Trump threatened on Saturday to push for legislation to compensate his allies if Cornyn and Tillis didn’t support Blanche. In recent days, the president also suggested he could temporarily withdraw Blanche’s nomination and reissue it after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office at the start of 2027.
The reversal by Blanche within 36 hours of that threat speaks to its lack of impact. Part of the problem Republicans want to avoid is having this damage the GOP's midterm prospects. The House will likely go to Democrats, thanks to the usual dynamics of midterm elections (and the 6.4-point gap in the current generic congressional ballot polling aggregate), but the Senate is still salvageable. Republicans need to put an end to the feuds and the controversies dogging the upper chamber and the White House. Otherwise, it's possible that Trump will awake on January 3rd to find out that none of his appointees have a prayer of winning confirmation, perhaps especially Blanche. The anti-weaponization fund and the plenary immunity from IRS audits are not worth that risk, especially if Trump has to replace a Supreme Court justice in his final two years in office.
Better to ask Congress to address the weaponization fund legislatively and end the feud now, rather than carry it into a Congress where Democrats control both chambers. This is a wiser move in the end, even if it doesn't exactly look like good news in the moment from the White House.

sources.news_title: Acting US Attorney General Blanche rescinds ‘anti-weaponization’ fund before confirmation vote - Regional Media News
sources.text:
Aug 2 (Reuters) – Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche rescinded an order establishing the “anti-weaponization” fund, paving the way for his confirmation ahead of a key Senate committee vote on Tuesday, after Republican senators stalled his nomination over concerns about the fund.
Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina had held up Blanche’s attorney general nomination while seeking written assurances that the Justice Department would not move forward with the fund, which critics have derided as a slush fund for Trump’s supporters.
“The Department of Justice today announced that the Acting Attorney General rescinded the May 18, 2026 Order that established “The Anti-Weaponization Fund,” according to a copy of the order Blanche by Blanche on X on Sunday.
The Republican senators had also objected to a Justice Department order that barred the Inland Revenue Service from pursuing any audits into past tax claims for Trump, his relatives and his companies for any tax returns filed before May 18.
“Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice, which will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS,” US media outlets quoted Natalie Yezbick, a spokesperson for Cornyn, as saying.
Blanche’s order stated that the tax order “applied by its terms only retroactively.”
“The Acting Attorney General stands by all of his July 15, 2026 Senate Judiciary Committee testimony, including answers to questions asked by Senator Cornyn related to the scope and applicability of the May 19, 2026 Order,” the DOJ statement shared by Blanche said, referring to the tax audit order.
Trump had said as recently as last week that the $1.8 “anti-weaponization” fund was dead.
However, the president said over the weekend that Blanche would stay in his current acting role if not confirmed by the Senate and added that he would also push Congress to codify the proposed “anti-weaponization” fund.
Tillis, whose term ends in January, wrote on Saturday that Blanche would not be confirmed because of Trump’s reversal, although he hoped that the matter could be resolved by Tuesday, when the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee has scheduled a nomination vote.
Blanche has served as acting attorney general since April, when Trump fired Pam Bondi.
The now-rescinded fund was created as part of a legal settlement between Trump and the U.S. Justice Department, to resolve his $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS over allegedly mishandling his tax records.
Supporters say the fund was intended to compensate individuals they argue were unfairly targeted by the federal government, while critics said it could direct taxpayer money to Trump allies, including those who assaulted police officers during the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot.
(Reporting by Shubham Kalia and Ananya Palyekar in Bengaluru; Editing by Lincoln Feast.)

sources.news_title: Acting AG Todd Blanche Scraps $1.8 Billion Trump Ally Fund, Clearing Senate Path - Tampa Free Press
sources.text:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal order late Sunday officially terminating President Donald Trump’s $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund,” resolving a weeks-long standoff with two Republican senators who had stalled his nomination to permanently lead the Justice Department.
The agreement sets up a Tuesday confirmation vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee. A spokeswoman for Texas Sen. John Cornyn confirmed the deal, while North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis did not immediately comment on the Sunday night release.
Cornyn and Tillis had withheld their support for Blanche over concerns regarding the fund, which was intended to compensate individuals who claimed they were unfairly prosecuted by previous administrations. Public and congressional pushback mounted over the possibility that violent rioters involved in the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack could receive financial payouts.
Although Blanche testified in June that the Justice Department would not implement the fund, Cornyn and Tillis insisted on seeing the commitment in writing before endorsing his nomination.
In a statement, Blanche said the order came after “good faith discussions” with members of Congress.
“My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche said.
The accompanying Justice Department order formally rescinds a May 18, 2026 order that created the framework for the fund. The document noted that “no Members were appointed; no funds were transferred; no process for receiving claims was established; no claims were paid,” adding that the official action “establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund.”
The document also narrows the scope of a separate provision from the settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS. The agreement clarifies that tax audit immunity for Trump and his family “applies by its terms only retroactively” to claims open at the time of the settlement, meaning it offers no protection against examinations of future tax filings.
The IRS settlement has faced significant scrutiny. On Friday, Trump’s lawyers notified a court that they would appeal a judge’s ruling that labeled the settlement an improper exercise in self-dealing. The judge in that case had criticized Blanche’s involvement due to his past work as Trump’s personal defense lawyer.
Throughout the negotiation process, President Trump continued to express support for compensating his allies. On Sunday evening, Trump argued that people charged in connection with the Jan. 6 Capitol riot had “their lives destroyed.”
“This would be a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered,” Trump said. “A lot of people like it.”
Trump had previously floated the idea of withdrawing Blanche’s nomination and resubmitting it next year after Cornyn, who lost a primary challenge, and Tillis, who is retiring, leave office.
Blanche joined the Justice Department last year as deputy attorney general and assumed the acting top role in April following the firing of former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

President Donald Trump said Monday that newly planned talks between the U.S. and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of U.S. strikes. Trump confirmed that the two countries were in contact and said he expects negotiations to address reopening the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. concerns about Iran’s nuclear program.
Trump said a day earlier he’d called off major strikes against Iran at the urging of Gulf allies, the latest in a pattern of threats and subsequent backpedaling from the U.S. president.
Meanwhile, 25 states sued the Trump administration Monday over its latest tariffs, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes the Supreme Court struck down in February. The U.S. last month imposed double-digit tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union just as the clock ran out on temporary tariffs Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court defeat.
Here is the latest:
Sen. Chuck Grassley invites former special counsel to testify about Trump investigation
Grassley says he has invited Jack Smith to testify before his panel on Sept. 22.
In a social media post announcing the invitation, Grassley, the chairman of the Republican-led committee, said that the American people “deserve nothing less than full transparency + accountability” related to the handling of the investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election.
Grassley wants to ask Smith about records showing that his team obtained phone records of some lawmakers on Capitol Hill, as well as the content of their text messages. Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, last month referred Smith to the Justice Department for a possible false statement investigation related to testimony about the records.
Lawyers for Smith say he testified truthfully and did nothing wrong.
Smith conducted two investigations into Trump, including related to his retention of classified records, that resulted in indictments. Both cases were abandoned after Trump won back the White House.
Trump Board of Peace officials meet congressional leaders as questions remain over Gaza peace plan
Members of President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace that is seeking and end to the Israel-Hamas conflict in Gaza met with U.S. officials and lawmakers in Washington on Monday.
The board members met with congressional staff and others to describe “current efforts to implement President Trump’s Comprehensive Peace Plan” and to work with Congress “to advance peace, security, governance, and reconstruction in Gaza.”
No details of the meeting were disclosed in a brief statement issued by the the Board of Peace.
The meeting took place as more senior officials from the Board of Peace met with top Israeli leaders in Israel.
25 states sue over Trump administration’s latest tariffs, citing Supreme Court ruling
Twenty-five states sued the Trump administration Monday over its latest tariffs, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes the Supreme Court struck down in February.
The United States last month imposed double-digit tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union, charging that they had not done enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor. The new tariffs took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary tariffs President Donald Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court defeat.
“After losing at the Supreme Court, the administration is once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs,” said New York Attorney General Letitia James.
Trump Washington surge opponents file complaint
A group of activists opposing the continued law enforcement and National Guard presence in Washington submitted a letter Monday to the D.C. Superior Court chief judge asking that he assess the seriousness and racial aspect of cases being brought by prosecutors during the surge.
Frankie Seabron, of CourtWatch DC, said 100 people a day were being taken into custody for minor crimes that would not have been pursued as vigorously before.
“Judges are not defenseless,” she said, “especially when they know prosecutors are abusing their powers.”
Seabron’s organization was one of several at a protest at Superior Court led by FreeDC. Ellen Hornstein with Lawyers Defending American Democracy also announced an ethics complaint had been filed last month against Jeanine Pirro with the Attorney Grievance Committee for the Supreme Court of the State of New York. The action cited her behavior in several cases, the reflecting pool vandalism case.
Trump says Pirro ‘folded like a cheap umbrella’
The president reiterated his disappointment with U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro for a court filing in which her office blamed a contractor’s shoddy work on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool rather than vandalism.
“I guess she choked. I don’t know what the hell happened,” Trump said, later adding that the former Fox News host “folded like a cheap umbrella” in moving to drop criminal charges against the former Olympian accused of deliberately damaging the pool.
Trump refused to say whether he’d move to fire Pirro. But he also acknowledged that the contractor was “rushing” to finish the project before July 4 — which didn’t ultimately happen.
And he suggested he “didn’t know” the contactor working on it, contradicting his own comments from April when he said he chose the company involved since it had performed work at his golf course in Virginia.
Trump avoids answering whether he supports MLB salary cap
Baseball’s collective bargaining agreement is set to expire Dec. 1 and there’s growing speculation that there could be a lockout that jeopardizes the 2027 season
The central point of contention is MLB owners push for a salary cap. Asked if he supported the owners push for a salary cap, Trump demurred.
“Well, we’re going to talk about that at a different time,” said Trump, a New York Yankees fan. “You know, it’s a complex situation, but not too complex for me.”
The president previously has suggested that he views salary caps in pro sports favorably. Trump in June told reporters that “if you don’t have a salary cap, you don’t have a sport” and suggested MLB “should have done it a long time ago.”
Trump says he looks forward to meeting DC’s new mayor
Trump said he’d welcome meeting with Janeese Lewis George, likely the next mayor of Washington, D.C., after he wrongly referred to her as a communist.
Lewis George is a self-described democratic socialist and a member of the D.C. Council who won the Democratic mayoral primary in June. In the overwhelmingly Democratic city, she is likely to take the top spot in November’s general election. She would succeed moderate Muriel Bowser, who decided to step down after three terms.
“I have not met her yet. I look forward to meeting her,” Trump said of Lewis George.
Trump says oil companies Chevron and Exxon Mobil made ‘too much money’
The U.S. president said major oil companies are earning excessive profits because of high oil prices.
“They made too much money, too much money, “ Trump said. “They ought to give some of that back to the public, and they better cut the retail price.”
Trump said he’s not happy with profits reported by Chevron and Exxon Mobil, even though the higher margins reflected energy prices that had increased after Trump launched a war with Iran and the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed to oil and natural gas tankers.
Trump’s predecessor in the White House, Democrat Joe Biden, also attacked oil companies for their profits when inflation was a major problem with voters.
Trump says he doesn’t know what was agreed to on to advance Blanche’s nomination
The president said, “I understand there’s been a sign off” but that “I don’t know what they agreed” to.
“I think Todd Blanche agreed to reconfirm things that he’s already said. And what he said was OK,” Trump added.
Two Republican Senators who had blocked the confirmation of Blanche, the acting attorney general, to lead the Justice Department said they’d reached an agreement to end the impasse.
Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis said they struck a deal to formally rescind the $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” that could have been used to compensate Trump supporters who overran the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
Despite saying he didn’t know the details of the deal to advance Blanche’s nomination, Trump defended the fund, saying his supporters had been “treated very unfairly.”
Trump defends his exemption from IRS audits because government was ‘weaponized’ against him
The U.S. president defended an agreement to exempt him, his sons and his business from tax audits.
The IRS had until Trump audited presidents since 1977, but the administration struck a deal to avoid audits of Trump as part of what was an initial agreement to end a lawsuit over the leaking of his tax records.
Trump said that before he ran for president in 2016 that an IRS audit of him had been settled. He said the audit was then reopened and he used it during the campaign a decade ago to justify not releasing his tax returns as other candidates have done.
“They went after me illegally and they did a lot of bad things to me like they did to other people,” Trump said. “It was weaponized against me.”
Trump says he’s leaving the Rep. Max Miller situation to the families involved
A day after telling reporters that he’d look into the allegations against the Ohio congressman, Trump said he’ll let the families “figure that out.”
“It’s a very sad thing,” Trump told reporters Monday in the Oval Office. “I know Max. He’s a good person.”
Miller is accused of domestic violence by his former wife, Emily Moreno, the daughter of Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno, who is close to Trump. Miller denies the allegations.
The senator said Sunday that his former son-in-law should not serve in Congress.
“You know, those families, I know they’re working on it. It’s a very sad thing,” Trump said. “Especially when you know somebody so well to be going through that. But it’s accusations, and I’m going to let them figure that out.”
Trump says new talks are ‘last chance’ for Iran to forge deal and avoid escalation of US strikes
President Donald Trump said Monday that newly planned talks with Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of U.S. strikes on the country.
Trump, speaking at the Oval Office, said he expects negotiations that will reopen the Strait of Hormuz and create a pathway for Iran to address United States’ concerns about it’s nuclear program will begin in the next day or two.
The Republican president says, “The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearization.” Trump says that ”will take a little while.”
While Trump has reveled in the U.S. military decimating layers of Tehran’s leadership and devastating its air force and navy, Iran is betting it can outlast Trump as he faces diminished stockpiles of munitions and the difficulty of executing a war that is unpopular with the American electorate ahead of November’s midterm election.
Trump signs executive order on military spouses
The order creates the “Presidential Military Spouse Commission” to address issues facing troops and their families. Jennifer Hegseth, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s wife, will lead it, Trump said.
The president said the new commission would “develop suggestions to address particular challenges in housing, employment, health care, education, child childcare and just about everything else you can think of.”
Many of the issues have been tackled in various forms by multiple administrations.
Jennifer Hegseth’s role mirrors that of other defense secretary spouses who have advocated for families while their husbands ran the Pentagon. Charlene Austin, Lloyd Austin’s wife, sat on the advisory boards for the Purdue Military Family Research Institute, and Military Child Education Coalition.
Trump calls Iran ‘unbelievably duplicitous’ with regard to peace talks
Trump is venting about the status of peace talks with Iran.
He criticized Iran’s leadership for claiming that its meetings with Oman on Monday were focused solely on establishing a temporary route for safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
The president previously said he held off on a massive weekend strike against Iran because there was another framework for a ceasefire and the full reopening of the strait to oil and natural gas tankers.
“Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous!” Trump posted on social media Monday. “They ask for a meeting, some would say “beg,” talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman.’”
Trump said whether “Iran wants to admit it or not, we are, in fact, talking” about preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons.
Breakneck pace in immigration courts is driving up deportation orders
The Trump administration is packing immigration courtrooms with speedier hearings to clear a decades-long backlog in asylum claims. New data shows a historic rise in missed court dates and immediate deportation orders as judges struggle to keep up the pace.
Hundreds of immigrants’ cases a day are being assigned to individual judges as the number of “mega” master hearings significantly increase. More than 1,300 were held in June alone, a nearly threefold jump from the previous June, according to Mobile Pathways, a nonprofit that tracks immigration court data.
The data also shows that courts have severely cut preparation time in complex immigration proceedings, so people are missing hearings and being told they’ve abandoned their asylum claims at unprecedented rates.
Those who favor limiting immigration see this as a course-correction for a longstanding problem. But the nonprofit’s chief operating officer says cases are being closed without being heard.
GOP holdouts say they will vote to advance Blanche’s nomination for attorney general
Two Republican senators who threatened to block acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s bid to lead the Justice Department said Monday that they will vote to advance his nomination, ending an impasse over plans to create a fund to compensate the president’s allies.
The statement from Republican Sen. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis came after Blanche issued an order late Sunday formally rescinding the $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” to compensate people who believe they were unfairly prosecuted by the Justice Department.
Cornyn and Tillis had said they would not support Blanche’s nomination without written confirmation that the fund is dead.
Trump stands to profit off US policy announcements by selling fast access to his social media posts
The president knows the world hangs on his every word. Now he wants you to pay for it.
Trump’s Truth Social business began selling sneak peeks of his social media posts on Saturday, offering early access to market-moving news to Wall Street traders willing to pay up. The move raises the prospect of big profits for Trump’s company, and big questions about insider trading and using public office for private gain.
Similar fast-speed feeds are sold by other social media firms and media providers, but Truth Social doesn’t just distribute the news, it makes it as Trump announces changes on everything from war to central bank leadership to tariffs.
“If this was the CEO of a public company, this would be jail time,” said Irene Aldridge, head of Able Alpha Trading.
Initial sales details may be disclosed when Truth Social’s parent company announces quarterly earnings.
Democrats’ future is at stake as El-Sayed and Stevens make final push in Michigan
Tuesday’s Senate primary in Michigan between congresswoman Haley Stevens and public health official Abdul El-Sayed is one of the clearest tests yet of where Democratic voters want their party to go.
El-Sayed is a progressive backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders who’s run against much of the Democratic establishment. Stevens is backed by Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and has made electability and experience central to her case.
The winner faces Republican Mike Rogers in November for an open seat Democrats likely need to hold to take control of the Senate next year.
Trump decries negative public polling and claims he’s never been more popular
The U.S. president said on social media that independent surveys showing low approval ratings are false — denying a clear trend of lower support for Trump because of inflation and the Iran war, among other issues.
“My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been,” Trump asserted, providing no data to back up his claim.
The AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 33% of U.S. adults approve of Trump. That survey from late July also showed a drop since the start of Trump’s second term in adults who “strongly approve” of him.
Contrary to the evidence of multiple surveys, Trump said his popularity is based on his income tax cuts, his job numbers, his efforts to secure the U.S. border with Mexico and his use of American military force in Venezuela and Iran.
Trump going to Los Angeles on Tuesday and speak in Las Vegas on Wednesday
The White House said the president will go to California and Nevada to talk up the economy and border security and slam Democrats ahead of the November elections.
Trump on Tuesday will attend a Republican National Committee dinner at the Trump National Golf Club in Los Angeles.
On Wednesday, the president is slated to talk about the economy at Red Rock Casino in Las Vegas.
Falling oil prices help calm Wall Street’s inflation worries, while chip stocks get back to sinking
Oil prices are easing and helping to calm Wall Street’s worries that inflation could potentially get even worse. That has U.S. stock indexes rising early Monday, but several major chip stocks are falling again including Micron and AMD.
The S&P 500 rose 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 625 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.2%. The price of a barrel of Brent crude fell 5.1% to $83.42 after Trump said over the weekend he would hold off on ordering new strikes against Iran at the urging of allies in the region. Treasury yields fell.
Trump overhaul could gut Head Start preschool quality standards
The Trump administration is planning a dramatic overhaul of Head Start that would gut its quality standards, two people familiar with the deliberations said.
Head Start, established in the 1960s to help fight poverty, has long been considered by experts to be a gold standard for early education. It has more than 100 pages of regulations that cover everything from child-to-teacher ratios and child health screenings to family engagement.
The Republicans would replace these with around a dozen pages of rules that leave most specifics to state and local law, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the information is not yet public and they feared reprisal.
The draft rules would require more documentation from homeless or unemployed parents, and an early version would have barred even the U.S. citizen children of parents who are in the United States illegally.

sources.news_title: Blanche rescinds $1.8 'anti-weaponization fund,' clearing key hurdle to AG confirmation
sources.text:
Blanche rescinds $1.8 'anti-weaponization fund,' clearing key hurdle to AG confirmation
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche is looking to smooth over contentious debate about his nomination for Attorney General after weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators surrounding the "anti-weaponization fund."
On Sunday evening, Blanche issued a formal order terminating President Donald Trump's $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund" to compensate political allies.
In a statement written on X, Blanche said the order came after several weeks of "good faith discussions."
My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions," Blanche said.
"The Department always welcomes and appreciates productive engagement with all members of Congress," Blanche said.
In a statement attached to Blanche's order, the DOJ explained that "although the Acting Attorney General has repeatedly advised Congress through testimony, including under oath, as well as in written responses, that the Fund is not moving forward, and the Department has repeatedly represented to district courts that the Fund is not moving forward, today’s Order officially rescinds the May 18, 2026 Order."
The agency said since the settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS, "No Members were appointed; no funds were transferred; no process for receiving claims was established; no claims were paid."
This order establishes, beyond any doubt, that there is no Fund."
Blanche's order also limits the scope of another provision of the settlement providing immunity for Trump and family members from tax audits. The deal states that the tax audit immunity agreement applies only retroactively to claims opened at the time of the settlement and doesn't protect Trump from future tax filing examination.
A spokesperson for Texas Republican Senator John Cornyn, who is one of the senators holding up Blanche's confirmation, confirmed the deal. North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis did not immediately comment.
The deal announcement comes ahead of a Tuesday confirmation vote for Blanche's AG nomination by the Senate Judiciary Committee. The vote was postponed last Thursday after Cornyn and Tillis demanded more time for the administration to clarify on the fund.
In a June hearing, Blanche said the Justice Department would not move forward with the fund, as bipartisan critics expressed concerns over the possibility that rioters who attacked police at the Capitol on July 6, 2021, could be considered for payments.
Cornyn and Tillis have said they wanted to see proof the fund would not move forward before they endorsed Blanche.
President Donald Trump has defended the fund, telling reporters on Air Force One Sunday evening that the fund would compensate those targeted by the DOJ under the Biden Administration.
People were hurt so badly. 22 suicides. And they were destroyed. Their families were destroyed for doing things that honestly there's never been an attack on any group of people in this country in my opinion, maybe one. There's one group that was attacked violently like these people were attacked and this would be a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered," Trump said. 
Trump said a lot of people like the fund, and if Blanche is not approved, he'd put it back on the table.
"A lot of people like it. A lot of big supporters of Trump like it," Trump said.
Trump previously said he would keep Blanche as acting attorney general should senators choose not to confirm him and pull his nomination until Cornyn and Tillis were out of office.
On Friday, Trump's attorneys notified the court that it would appeal a judge's ruling that characterized the settlement of his IRS lawsuit as "an improper exercise in self-dealing."
__________
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Blanche Nears Confirmation as AG After Killing Off $1.8B Weaponization Payout Fund › American Greatness
sources.text:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche moved a step closer to Senate confirmation Sunday after formally scrapping a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” and tightening the tax protections tied to President Donald Trump’s IRS settlement, a move that appears to have satisfied two Republican holdouts who had stalled his nomination.
A spokeswoman for Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, confirmed Sunday that the Justice Department had reached an agreement with Cornyn, who along with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., had blocked Blanche’s confirmation. The deal clears the way for Cornyn to back Blanche when the Senate Judiciary Committee votes Tuesday. Tillis had not publicly weighed in on the agreement as of Sunday night, though he is expected to follow Cornyn’s lead.
Republicans need every member of the committee on board Tuesday to overcome unified Democratic opposition to Blanche’s nomination. An earlier committee vote was postponed after Cornyn and Tillis demanded a written commitment from the administration before moving forward.
Blanche met those demands by terminating the fund outright and clarifying that tax protections in the settlement apply only retroactively, not to future filings. The Justice Department said the fund never became operational. No members were appointed, no money changed hands, no claims process existed and no payments were ever made.
“My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche wrote on X Sunday. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement. The Department always welcomes and appreciates productive engagement with all members of Congress.”
Blanche’s order rescinded the May 18 directive that established the fund. Cornyn and Tillis had pushed for written assurances after Trump kept voicing support for the idea publicly, and after lawmakers raised alarm that people convicted in the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot could have been eligible for payouts under the original plan.
“Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice, which will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS,” Cornyn spokeswoman Natalie Yezbick told Politico.
Tillis had voiced sharp frustration Saturday, before the agreement came together, accusing Trump of intending to “resurrect the payout pot” through a new fund or by pushing Congress toward a bill most Senate Republicans opposed. “It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal. Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday,” Tillis said at the time.
Blanche has served as acting attorney general since taking over for Pam Bondi in April. Senate Republicans are hoping to push his nomination through before the end of the week.

Acting US Attorney-General Todd Blanche rescinded an order establishing the "anti-weaponization" fund, paving the way for his confirmation ahead of a key Senate committee vote on Tuesday, after Republican senators stalled his nomination over concerns about the fund.
Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina had held up Blanche's attorney general nomination while seeking written assurances that the Justice Department would not move forward with the fund, which critics have derided as a slush fund for Trump's supporters.

"Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice, which will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS,” US media outlets quoted Natalie Yezbick, a spokesperson for Cornyn, as saying.
Push for Congress to codify anti-weaponization fund
Blanche's order stated that the tax order "applied by its terms only retroactively."

Blanche rescinds fund for Trump allies, removing threat to his attorney general bid
WASHINGTON — Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal order late Sunday formally rescinding President Donald Trump’s $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” to compensate his political allies after Senate Republicans threatened to block his nomination to become attorney general over the controversial deal.
“My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche posted on X. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement.”
A spokeswoman for Texas Sen. John Cornyn, one of the senators holding up Blanche’s nomination, confirmed the deal, which comes ahead of a Tuesday confirmation vote for Blanche’s nomination in the Senate Judiciary Committee. The other GOP senator, North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis, did not have immediate comment.
Blanche, who is serving as acting chief of the Justice Department, attached an order dated Sunday to his post that said, “The Attorney General’s May 18, 2026 Order establishing the Anti-Weaponization Fund (‘Fund’) is rescinded and shall have nor force or effect.”
The controversial fund — created as part of an agreement to settle a lawsuit from Trump against the IRS — was at the center of resistance to Blanche’s nomination from Cornyn and Tillis, who sit on the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Blanche had already said the fund was “dead,” and the Justice Department told courts the program was abandoned, but officials have previously declined to put the commitment in writing. The fund would have offered taxpayer money to people who claimed they were victims of weaponization by the federal government — including those involved with the January 6, 2021, US Capitol riot.
The document released Sunday also limits the addendum to that agreement that offers the president and members of his family immunity from tax investigations — a sticking point for Cornyn. The senator wanted Blanche to explicitly acknowledge that it applies only to past tax investigations against the president and those listed in the IRS lawsuit.
The Sunday order says the measure “applies by its terms only retroactively” and that it applies only to “the named parties in the lawsuit” referenced in the agreement.
Blanche’s announcement comes after a week of uncertainty over his confirmation to the attorney general role. Trump on Thursday threatened to temporarily pull the nomination amid the resistance from Tillis and Cornyn, and renominate Blanche after they leave the Senate next year. The senators met privately with Blanche Thursday afternoon though they did not reach a deal.
The president said Cornyn and Tillis were “both upset because I wouldn’t endorse them.” Cornyn lost his primary this spring to Trump-backed firebrand Ken Paxton. Tillis, a frequent Trump critic, decided last year not to run for reelection.
The demands left Blanche in a difficult place, since putting limits on the tax addendum could anger the president.
Trump then said Saturday he would push to get the “anti-weaponization” passed into law if he couldn’t garner the support in the Senate to confirm Blanche, his former personal lawyer. Tillis responded to that threat by saying Blanche, “who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal.”
Even just hours before Blanche’s Sunday announcement, Trump defended the controversial “anti-weaponization” fund and reiterated that if the Senate doesn’t confirm Blanche, he will put the idea “back on the table.”
“A lot of people like it. … If they don’t approve Todd, I put it back on the table,” he told reporters on Air Force One.
Trump said the fund “would be a reimbursement for the pain” his supporters and allies who would be eligible for the fund “suffered.”

sources.news_title: Cornyn Strikes Deal Clearing Path For Blanche AG Vote
sources.text:
Cornyn Strikes Deal Clearing Path For Blanche AG Vote
Todd Blanche moved closer to becoming the next attorney general on Sunday night after Senator John Cornyn announced that he had struck an agreement with the Department of Justice over a disputed settlement tied to President Donald Trump. The breakthrough resolves a standoff that had put Blanche’s nomination in doubt just days before a scheduled Senate Judiciary Committee vote.
Table of Contents
What The Cornyn Strikes Deal Actually Changes
Cornyn’s office confirmed that the agreement requires the Justice Department to formally cancel a controversial one point eight billion dollar fund that had been created as part of a broader settlement Trump reached with the IRS earlier this year. Critics referred to the fund informally as a payout pool meant to compensate Trump aligned political figures.
Under the new arrangement announced by Cornyn’s spokesperson Natalie Yezbick the DOJ will issue a binding written order permanently shutting down that fund. The order also narrows a separate IRS audit immunity provision so that it only covers the individuals who were actual plaintiffs in the underlying lawsuit including Trump himself rather than extending protection more broadly to his family or associates.
Blanche confirmed the terms in a post on X shared the same evening. He said his team had worked through the outstanding concerns raised by senators and had issued an order stating the disputed fund is rescinded and carries no legal force going forward. He added that the department’s official interpretation of the audit settlement limits its reach strictly to the named parties in the case.
A Tense 72 Hour Standoff Before Tuesday’s Vote
The agreement follows roughly three days of public friction between Trump and Cornyn. Trump had criticized the Texas senator repeatedly and expressed frustration that the fund meant to benefit his allies had already been pulled back. At one point Trump floated a more drastic option suggesting he could withdraw Blanche’s nomination altogether and simply resubmit it at a later date once Cornyn and fellow Republican critic Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina were no longer in Congress.
That threat added pressure to an already delicate political calculation. The Senate Judiciary Committee is scheduled to vote on Blanche’s nomination Tuesday and with every Democrat on the panel opposed a single Republican no vote could have doomed his chances entirely. Cornyn had positioned himself as that potential deciding vote making his objections to the IRS settlement a genuine obstacle rather than a symbolic protest.
Tillis Signals He Will Follow Cornyn’s Lead
Tillis another swing vote on the committee had also expressed reservations about the settlement in the days leading up to the deal. In a post shared Saturday on X he said it appeared Trump intended to revive what he described as a payout fund for political allies. He added that he still considered Blanche qualified for the role and called it unfortunate that the nomination risked stalling over the dispute while expressing hope the matter would be settled before Tuesday’s meeting.
With Cornyn’s agreement now in place Tillis is expected to support moving the nomination forward as well clearing what had been the last major hurdle standing between Blanche and committee approval.
Path To Confirmation Now Clear For Blanche
Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since April when Pam Bondi stepped down from the role. Senate Republican leadership has said it wants a final confirmation vote completed before the end of the week assuming Tuesday’s committee proceedings go smoothly.
The episode highlights how a single senator’s objections tied to a contested financial settlement can slow even a nomination with broad party support. Cornyn’s insistence on written and binding language rather than informal assurances appears to have been the key sticking point throughout the negotiations and now stands as the mechanism that unlocked Blanche’s path toward full Senate confirmation.

sources.news_title: Acting US Attorney General Blanche rescinds ‘anti-weaponization’ fund before confirmation vote
sources.text:
By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff
Aug 3 (Reuters) – Two key Republican senators said on Monday they would support Todd Blanche’s nomination for U.S. attorney general, paving the way for his confirmation after reaching a deal that would rescind an “anti-weaponization” package widely criticized as a slush fund for supporters of President Donald Trump.
Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina had held up Blanche’s nomination as they sought written confirmation that the Justice Department would not move forward with the $1.8 billion fund. Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump now serving as acting attorney general, posted a statement on social media on Sunday saying the fund had been rescinded.
“We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon,” Cornyn and Tillis said in a joint statement.
Their support likely enables the committee to advance Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday. A vote by the full Senate could come as early as Saturday, unless Democrats agree to an earlier vote.
The agreement appears to resolve one of the highest-profile Republican challenges to Trump in Congress, led by the two lawmakers. Tillis is retiring in January and Cornyn lost his primary for the Republican nomination after Trump endorsed other Senate candidates in each of their states.
The fund was created as part of a legal settlement to resolve a $10 billion lawsuit Trump filed against his own government, alleging that the Internal Revenue Service had mishandled his tax records.
Supporters say the fund was intended to compensate individuals they argue were unfairly targeted by the federal government. Critics, including Tillis and Cornyn, said it could direct taxpayer money to Trump allies, including those who assaulted police officers during the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot.
Trump said Monday he was aware that the two Republican senators said they will vote to advance Blanche’s nomination.
“I understand there’s been a sign-off, but … I don’t know what they agreed,” Trump told reporters. “I think Todd Blanche agreed to reconfirm things that he’s already said, and what he said was OK.”
PAST TAX CLAIMS
The Republican senators had also objected to a related order that barred the IRS from auditing past tax returns for Trump, his relatives and his companies for any tax returns filed before May 18. They said they wanted clarifications to narrow to whom and how it applied to ensure that Trump did not receive blanket tax immunity forever.
Blanche obliged, specifying that it only applies to Trump, his sons and the family business, and that their future tax returns could still be investigated.
“The Department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the Treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share,” Tillis and Cornyn said.
Blanche’s order stated that the tax order “applied by its terms only retroactively.” Critics of the Blanche order said immunity for Trump’s past tax returns could still save the president millions, and that the settlement agreement requires the approval of both sides, including Trump’s personal lawyers, to change it. Trump’s personal lawyers did not sign the order and have not publicly commented on the decision.
“They don’t pull back on the ongoing attempts to give the President, his family, and his affiliates unauthorized immunity from tax audits,” Brandon DeBot, policy director at the nonpartisan Tax Law Center, said in a statement. “They don’t do anything new to stop the President from trying to bring back the fund, as he threatened to this weekend.”
Blanche has served as acting attorney general since April, when Trump fired Pam Bondi.
(Reporting by Shubham Kalia and Ananya Palyekar in Bengaluru and Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff in Washington; Editing by Andy Sullivan, Alistair Bell and Rod Nickel)

sources.news_title: Trump supporters' anti-weaponisation fund scrapped
sources.text:
Trump supporters' anti-weaponisation fund scrapped
US Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche has issued a formal order terminating President Donald Trump's $US1.8 billion ($A2.6 billion) "anti-weaponisation fund" to compensate his political allies.
The move follows weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney-general.
A spokeswoman for Texas Senator John Cornyn, one of the senators holding up Blanche's nomination, confirmed the agreement late on Sunday. The other GOP senator, North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis, did not have immediate comment.
The announcement comes as a Senate Judiciary Committee vote on Blanche is scheduled for Tuesday.
"My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions," Blanche said in a post on X.
"We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order."
The order says that "although the Acting Attorney General has repeatedly advised Congress through testimony, including under oath, as well as in written responses, that the Fund is not moving forward, and the Department has repeatedly represented to district courts that the Fund is not moving forward, today's Order officially rescinds the May 18, 2026 Order:
The document released by Blanche on Sunday night also limits the scope of another provision of the settlement stemming from a lawsuit Trump filed against the Internal Revenue Service that provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits.
It clarifies that the tax audit immunity agreement "applies only retroactively" to claims open at the time of the settlement and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings.
While Blanche has repeatedly said publicly that the fund was dead, the Justice Department had resisted formally confirming that in writing. That had drawn concern from lawmakers that it could be revived in some form, especially after Trump expressed continued support for the idea.
The two sides have been negotiating for weeks, but Trump has said repeatedly during the talks that he thinks the fund should go forward.
Earlier on Sunday evening, Trump said that people who had faced charges from the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol and could have benefitted from the fund had "their lives destroyed".
"This would be a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered," Trump said.
"A lot of people like it."

sources.news_title: Blanche’s AG nomination back on track after he formally rescinds payout fund
Key GOP holdouts say they’ll back Blanche for attorney general after he rescinded Trump’s ‘anti-weaponization’ fund
sources.text:
Two key Senate Republicans said Monday they will back Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s nominee for attorney general, after he rescinded the president’s “anti-weaponization” fund.
Blanche’s order late Sunday formally rescinding the president’s $1.8 billion fund ended an impasse with the senators, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas, who threatened to block his nomination over the controversial agreement.
“My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche posted on X. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order and update with regard to the May IRS settlement.”
Blanche, who is serving as acting chief of the Justice Department, attached an order dated Sunday to his post that said, “The Attorney General’s May 18, 2026 Order establishing the Anti-Weaponization Fund (‘Fund’) is rescinded and shall have nor force or effect.”
The controversial fund — created as part of an agreement to settle a lawsuit from Trump against the IRS — was at the center of resistance to Blanche’s nomination from Cornyn and Tillis, who sit on the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The senators said in a joint statement Monday they were “pleased” with Blanche’s order and they “look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon.”
Blanche had already said the fund was “dead,” and the Justice Department told courts the program was abandoned, but officials have previously declined to put the commitment in writing. The fund would have offered taxpayer money to people who claimed they were victims of weaponization by the federal government — including those involved with the January 6, 2021, US Capitol riot.
The document released Sunday also limits the addendum to that agreement that offers the president and members of his family immunity from tax investigations — a sticking point for Cornyn. The senator wanted Blanche to explicitly acknowledge that it applies only to past tax investigations against the president and those listed in the IRS lawsuit.
The Sunday order says the measure “applies by its terms only retroactively” and that it applies only to “the named parties in the lawsuit” referenced in the agreement.
Tillis and Cornyn said in their statement that the acknowledgement addressed “concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.”
The settlement agreement is a contract between the Justice Department and Trump. The document released Sunday was notably signed only by Blanche, but not by Trump or his personal lawyers.
The Senate Judiciary Committee will vote Tuesday on Blanche’s nomination, meaning he could be confirmed before the chamber leaves for a five-week recess.
Blanche’s announcement comes after a week of uncertainty over his confirmation to the attorney general role. Trump on Thursday threatened to temporarily pull the nomination amid the resistance from Tillis and Cornyn, and renominate Blanche after they leave the Senate next year. The senators met privately with Blanche Thursday afternoon, and three sources familiar with the matter previously told CNN they made progress, though they did not reach a deal.
The president said Cornyn and Tillis were “both upset because I wouldn’t endorse them.” Cornyn lost his primary this spring to Trump-backed firebrand Ken Paxton. Tillis, a frequent Trump critic, decided last year not to run for reelection.
The demands left Blanche in a difficult place, since putting limits on the tax addendum could anger the president.
Trump then said Saturday he would push to get the “anti-weaponization” fund passed into law if he couldn’t garner the support in the Senate to confirm Blanche, his former personal lawyer. Tillis responded to that threat by saying Blanche, “who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal.”
Just hours before Blanche’s Sunday announcement, Trump defended the controversial “anti-weaponization” fund and reiterated that if the Senate doesn’t confirm Blanche, he will put the idea “back on the table.”
Trump told reporters on Air Force One that the fund “would be a reimbursement for the pain” his supporters and allies who would be eligible for the fund “suffered.”
CNN has reached out to the White House for comment on Blanche’s order.
This story and headline have been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Manu Raju contributed to this report.
